{{Short description|Stochastic process for effort or wear}}
{{About|the stochastic process|the astrophysical process|Gamma process (astrophysics)}}
[[File:Gamma-Process.png|thumb|326x326px|Two different gamma processes from time 0 until time 4. The red process has more occurrences in the timeframe compared to the blue process because its ''shape'' parameter is larger than the blue shape parameter.]]
A '''gamma process''', also called the ''Moran-Gamma subordinator'',{{sfn|Klenke|2008|p=536}} is a two-parameter [[stochastic process]] which models the accumulation of ''effort'' or ''wear'' over time. The gamma process has [[independent increments|independent]] and [[stationary increments]] which follow the [[gamma distribution]], hence the name. The gamma process is studied in [[mathematics]], [[statistics]], [[probability theory]], and [[stochastic]]s, with particular applications in [[deterioration modeling]]{{sfn|Sánchez-Silva|Klutke|2016|p=93}} and [[mathematical finance]].{{sfn|Fu|Madan|2007|p=38}}

== Notation ==

The gamma process is often abbreviated as <math>X(t)\equiv\Gamma(t;\gamma, \lambda)</math> where <math>t</math> represents the time from 0. The shape parameter <math>\gamma</math> (inversely) controls the jump size, and the rate parameter <math>\lambda</math> controls the rate of jump arrivals, analogously with the gamma distribution.{{sfn|Sánchez-Silva|Klutke|2016|p=133}} Both <math>\gamma</math> and <math>\lambda</math> must be greater than 0. We use the [[gamma function]] and [[gamma distribution]] in this article, so the reader should distinguish between <math>\Gamma(\cdot)</math> (the gamma function), <math>\Gamma(\gamma, \lambda)</math> (the gamma distribution), and <math>\Gamma(t;\gamma, \lambda)</math> (the gamma process).

== Definition ==

The process is a pure-jump [[increasing]] [[Lévy process]] with intensity measure <math>\nu(x)=\gamma x^{-1} \exp(-\lambda x),</math> for all positive <math>x</math>. It is assumed that the process starts from a value 0 at <math>t=0</math> meaning <math>X(0)=0</math>. Thus jumps whose size lies in the interval <math>[x,x+dx)</math> occur as a [[Poisson process]] with intensity <math>\nu(x)\,dx.</math>

The process can also be defined as a stochastic process <math>X(t), t \leq 0</math> with <math>X(0) = 0</math> and independent increments, whose [[marginal distribution]] <math>f</math> of the random variable <math>X(t) - X(s)</math> for an increment <math>l = t-s \geq 0</math> is given by{{sfn|Sánchez-Silva|Klutke|2016|p=133}}
<math display="block">f(x;l, \gamma, \lambda) = \Gamma(\gamma l, \lambda) = \frac {\lambda^{\gamma l}}{\Gamma (\gamma l)} x^{\gamma l-1}e^{-\lambda x}.</math>

=== Inhomogenous process ===

It is also possible to allow the shape parameter <math>\gamma</math> to vary as a function of time, <math>\gamma(t)</math>.{{sfn|Sánchez-Silva|Klutke|2016|p=133}}

==Properties==
{{RefImprove|section|date=June 2023}}
=== Mean and variance ===
Because the value at each time <math>t</math> has mean <math>\gamma t/\lambda</math> and variance <math>\gamma t/\lambda^2,</math>{{sfn|Sánchez-Silva|Klutke|2016|p=94}} the gamma process is sometimes also parameterised in terms of the mean (<math>\mu</math>) and variance (<math>v</math>) of the increase per unit time. These satisfy <math>\gamma = \mu^2/v</math> and <math>\lambda = \mu/v</math>. 

=== Scaling ===
Multiplication of a gamma process by a scalar constant <math>\alpha</math> is again a gamma process with different mean increase rate.
<math display="block">\alpha\Gamma(t;\gamma,\lambda) \simeq \Gamma(t;\gamma,\lambda/\alpha)</math>

=== Adding independent processes ===
The sum of two independent gamma processes is again a gamma process.
<math display="block">\Gamma(t;\gamma_1,\lambda) + \Gamma(t;\gamma_2,\lambda) \simeq \Gamma(t;\gamma_1+\gamma_2,\lambda)</math>

=== Moments ===
The [[Moment (mathematics)|moment function]] helps mathematicians find expected values, variances, skewness, and kurtosis.
<math display="block">\operatorname E(X_t^n) = \lambda^{-n} \cdot \frac{\Gamma(\gamma t+n)}{\Gamma(\gamma t)},\ \quad n\geq 0 ,</math>   where <math>\Gamma(z)</math> is the [[Gamma function]].

=== Moment generating function ===
The [[Moment-generating function|moment generating function]] is the expected value of <math>\exp(tX)</math> where X is the [[random variable]].
<math display="block">\operatorname E\Big(\exp(\theta X_t)\Big) = \left(1- \frac\theta\lambda\right)^{-\gamma t},\  \quad \theta<\lambda</math>

=== Correlation ===
[[Correlation]] displays the statistical relationship between any two gamma processes.  
<math display="block">\operatorname{Corr}(X_s, X_t) = \sqrt{\frac s t},\ s<t</math>, for any gamma process <math>X(t) .</math>

== Related processes ==

The gamma process is used as the distribution for random time change in the [[variance gamma process]]. Specifically, combining Brownian motion with a gamma process produces a variance gamma process,{{sfn|Applebaum|2004|pp=58-59}} and a variance gamma process can be written as the difference of two gamma processes.{{sfn|Fu|Madan|2007|p=38}}
